newsitem.title: INDIA: New Congress chief is follower of Mahatma Gandhi.
newsitem.headline: New Congress chief is follower of Mahatma Gandhi.

text.p: Sitaram Kesri, chosen by senior leaders on Monday as provisional president of India's Congress party, is a veteran who was jailed many times during India's struggle for independence.
Former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned on Saturday as the president of India's oldest party. Kesri, 76, will be stopgap chief until a party plenary next month.
Rao quit after a court asked him to testify in a case of criminal conspiracy involving a businessman who claims he paid $100,000 to a friend of Rao in 1983 in a failed bid to win a state contract.
Rao says he is innocent but resigned to help his party, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947.
Kesri was a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi and has a stature that inspires awe even among senior Congressmen. His name was proposed by Rao himself.

As a student, Kesri, who comes from the mineral rich but economically backward state of Bihar, quit studying to join the freedom movement. Jailed by the British, he even refused parole to attend his father's funeral rites.
Many believe that Kesri's roots in the movement and his amiable disposition could help him bind togther the party which led India to freedom but now stuck finds support dwindling.

In a party which rivals say is too strongly oriented towards the Hindu upper castes and the rich, Kesri has been an outspoken supporter of job quotas in government as affirmative action to help low castes. He also champions protection for minority Moslems.
Kesri has been the party's treasurer since 1979, and has raised funds for the Congress to fight four general elections, but has personally been never charged with corruption.

As a backroom strategist, he has also worked closely with party chiefs and prime ministers of differing styles, from the imperious Indira Gandhi, her impatient son, Rajiv and the laid-back and reticent Rao.
Kesri has been a minister under all three.
Jovial, earthy and fond of dogs, his visible side does not quite match his repuatation of a shrewd thinker.
But many who have watched India's oldest party say that he is a weathercock who has often sensed the direction the complex organisation would take after its frequent tussles among ambitious leaders.
